To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ethanol significantly increases the hepatic clearance of DRV but not intracellular total DRV concentrations in HIV-infected monocytes.
ethanol exposure increased hepical intrinsic clearance of DRV and decreased its inhibitory potency in HIV-infected monocytes.
ethanol significantly increased the hepatic intrinsic clearance of RTV- and DRV-boosted DRV, but had no significant influence on total DRV exposure in HIV-infected monocytes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the potential interactions between ethanol and DRV in the liver and in HIV-infected monocytes.
the potential interactions between DRV and ethanol, which may be relevant to HIV-infected patients who consume alcohol regularly.
the impact of ethanol on DRV pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in HIV-monocytes and its potential interactions with CYP3A.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ethanol has an inhibitory effect on the metabolism of RTV-Boosted DRV, but this effect is limited and not clinically significant.
ethanol exposure increases the risk of drug interactions with RTV-boosting DRV in the liver.
ethanol has a limited effect on DRV metabolism and intracellular bioavailability in HIV-infected monocytes, but it may increase DRV degradation and clearance in liver microsomes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

alcohol consumption may alter DRV metabolism in the liver but not in the HIV-infected cells, and this may lead to altered pharmacokinetics and/or drug-drug interactions in HIV+ people who drink alcohol.
ethanol may increase the bioavailability of DRV, but this effect is limited in the presence of HIV.
ethanol exposure increases DRV metabolism in the liver but not in monocytes, which may have implications for the use of DRV in HIV-infected people with alcohol use disorder.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ethanol may alter the pharmacokinetics of DRV, which may lead to reduced efficacy of the drug in HIV-infected individuals.
the inhibitory potency of darunavir against CYP3A is significantly reduced by ethanol, which may lead to increased bioavailability and toxicity of other CYP3A substrates.
ethanol exposure may increase the risk for DRV failure in HIV-infected people.
